(Per Hon'ble Sri Justice Vakiti Ramakrishna Reddy) This Appeal, filed by the APSRTC (presently TGSRTC) under Section 54 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 (for short, "the Act"), is directed against the judgment and award dated 18.07.2002 passed in O.P. No. 40 of 1991 on the file of Senior Civil Judge, at Suryapet (hereinafter called as 'Reference Court), whereby the Reference Court enhanced the compensation awarded by the Land Acquisition Officer (for short, "LAO") in respect of the acquired land.

I. BRIEF FACTS:
2.

The lands situated in Survey No. 787 to an extent of Ac. 1.17 guntas of wet land of Claimant No.1,
Survey No. 789 to an extent of Ac. 1.07 guntas and Ac. 1.07 guntas of Claimant No.2 and 3 situated in Kodad Mandal headquarters, were acquired for the purpose of construction of bus depot at Mandal Headquarters.
A notification under Section 4(1) of the Act was published on 03.02.1987.

3. The LAO passed an award dated 25.05.1990 fixing the market value of acquired lands at Rs.
33,333/- per acre for wet land of Claimant No.1 and Rs. 28,888/- per acre for the dry Bagayath land of Claimant No.2 and 3.
Not being satisfied with the said compensation, the claimants sought a reference under Section 18 of the Act before the Reference Court.

II. POINTS FOR CONSIDERATION BEFORE THE  REFERENCE COURT:
A.P.S.R.T.C vs Tammara Ahalya on 5 March, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/65854664/
1 4.

The following Point for consideration was framed for determination by the Reference Court:
1) Whether the Compensation awarded by the Land Acquisition Officer is not just and proper and if so, the same needs to be enhanced and if so at what relief?
2) To what result?
III. EVIDENCE ON RECORD:
5.
Before the Reference Court, the claimants examined PWs 1 to 6 and marked Exs.A1 to A9, which included exemplar sale deeds relating to the adjacent lands.
On behalf of the respondents, RWs 1 and 2 were examined and Ex. B1 to B6 were marked.

IV. FINDINGS OF THE REFERENCE COURT:
6.

Upon appreciation of the oral and documentary evidence on record, the Reference Court observed that the acquired land, though classified as agricultural, possessed substantial non-agricultural and commercial potential owing to its strategic location abutting National Highway No.9, immediate proximity to the RTC Bus Stand and Bus Depot, and the presence of educational institutions,
government offices, markets, industries, and dense residential developments in and around Kodad Town.

entities.label: ORG

sentences.text: It was further observed that the land could not be valued merely as wet or dry agricultural land and that its urban character and building potential had to be taken into consideration while determining the market value.

7. The Reference Court also observed that the sale transactions relied upon by the claimants under Exs.A4 to A7 were genuine and comparable, and could be used as guiding factors to ascertain the prevailing market value, whereas the sale deeds marked under Exs.B2 to B5 by the respondents were not comparable due to lack of proximity and similarity.

Taking into account the escalation trend reflected in the documents of the claimants' and the report of Advocate Commissioner, the Reference Court fixed the market value of acquired land at Rs. 141.12/- per square yard (i.e., Rs.
5,57,568/- per acre) with statutory benefits, by allowing a deduction at a rate of 20% towards developmental charges, as on the date of notification.
8. Aggrieved by the order dated 18.06.2002 passed by the Reference Court, the APSRTC has preferred the present Appeal.

V. SUBMISSIONS OF THE PARTIES:
a) Submissions on behalf of the Appellant:
9.
The learned Standing Counsel for APSRTC appearing for the appellant contends that the judgment and decree of the Reference Court are contrary to law and the evidence on record.

The Reference Court erred in enhancing the compensation to Rs.141.12/- per square yard (i.e., Rs.
5,57,568/- per acre) for the lands in Sy.No.787 and Sy.No.789, despite the fact that the A.P.S.R.T.C vs Tammara Ahalya on 5 March, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/65854664/
2 compensation awarded by the LAO was based on similar sale exemplars.

It is further contended that having noticed that the first claimant himself claimed compensation at Rs. 7,00,000/- per acre during the award enquiry (which works out to Rs. 144.62 per square yard), and having held that deduction towards development charges was necessary, the Reference Court erred in deducting only 20%, whereas at least 40% deduction ought to have been applied.
10.

The learned Standing Counsel further submits that the sale transactions relied upon by the claimants are not comparable, as the lands covered thereunder are situated far away from the acquired land and lies in more developed localities.
It is also urged that the Reference Court relied mostly on the post-notification sale transactions.

It is settled law that only comparable sale transactions within three years prior to the Section 4(1) notification can be considered, and the post-notification developments and constructions cannot be taken into account.
11. On the basis of the aforesaid submissions, the learned Standing Counsel has prayed that, the compensation enhanced by the Reference Court is excessive, erroneous, and liable to be set aside.
It is also urged that there being merit in the appeal, the same may be allowed.

b) Submissions on behalf of the Respondents:
12.

The learned Counsel appearing for the respondents/claimants on the other hand submitted that the lands are situated immediately to the southern side of the existing RTC Bus Stand and abutting National Highway No.9, and were acquired for construction of the RTC Bus Depot itself, which clearly establishes that the land possessed substantial commercial and non-agricultural potential even as on the date of the Section 4(1) notification dated 03.02.1987.

The acquired lands being surrounded by the educational institutions, government offices, markets, and residential colonies in Kodad town demonstrates that the land had already assumed an urban character, and therefore,
valuation on par with ordinary agricultural lands was not lawful.

13. The learned counsel for the respondents further contended that the sale transactions marked as Exs.A4 and A7, relate to lands in Kodad Town abutting NH-9 and the existing Bus Stand, hence,
they are comparable in situation and potentiality to the acquired lands.

In contrast, the sale deeds relied upon by the appellants under Exs.B2 to B5 pertain to the lands located in interior agricultural areas, not abutting the National Highway, and lacking similar commercial advantages.

It was further urged that the documents which are subsequent to the Notification under section 4(1) of the Act does not render them irrelevant, as they were relied upon only to ascertain the trend of escalation in land values in Kodad.

It was further contended that the Reference Court fixed the compensation at a rate of Rs.141.12/- per square yard was arrived at after making a conscious deduction of 20%
towards development charges, which is reasonable in the present case, as the land was acquired for an RTC Bus Depot and not for formation of residential layouts requiring extensive internal roads and amenities.

It was also submitted that the compensation awarded does not exceed the claim originally made by the respondents during the award enquiry and adequately balances the interests of both parties, therefore, the enhancement granted is reasonable and lawful and calls for no interference in appeal.

VI. ISSUES FOR CONSIDERATION:
16. Having heard the learned counsel appearing for the respective parties and having carefully examined the material placed on record, the following issues arise for determination in this Appeal:
(i) Whether the Reference Court was justified in enhancing the market value of the acquired lands?
(ii) Whether the enhancement granted is in accordance with law and supported by evidence on record?
(iii) To what reliefs are the claimants entitled?

From the above tabulation and on a careful consideration of the evidence, it is manifest that the LAO had adopted a just and judicial approach in fixing the market value of the acquired lands, by taking note of the following:
i. the location, surroundings and potentiality of the lands; and ii. the sale exemplars of the proximate period.
VIII. ANALYSIS:
19.

On a careful and independent appreciation of the oral and documentary evidence on record, this Court finds that the acquisition of Acs.3-32 guntas in Sy.Nos.787 and 789 of Kodad Town for construction of the A.P.S.R.T.C. Bus Depot pursuant to the notification under Section 4(1) dated 03.02.1987 is not in dispute.
The classification of Ac.1-17 guntas. in Sy.No.787 as wet land and Acs.2- 15 guntas in Sy. No.789 as dry land is also admitted.
The LAO, by Award dated 25.05.1990 (Ex. B-1), fixed the market value of the acquired lands at Rs.33,333/- per acre in respect of wet land and Rs.28,888/- per acre in respect of dry land.
The claimants received the compensation under protest and sought reference under Section 18.
The issue, therefore, revolves solely around the rate of market value as on the date of notification.

[

21. At the outset, it is necessary to examine the evidentiary value and relevancy of Ex. A-4, which has been strongly relied upon by the claimants for determination of fair market value of the lands acquired.

The admissibility, proximity in time, comparability in situation, and genuineness of the said document are required to be scrutinized in the light of the settled principles governing assessment of compensation under the Land Acquisition Act.
22. Ex.A-4 is a certified copy of a registered sale deed dated 05.06.1984 in respect of land to an extent of 117 1/3 square yards situated in Ward No.1 of Kodad Gram Panchayat.
The transaction reflects a consideration at the rate of Rs.200/- per square yard.

The sale is prior to the Section 4(1)
Notification dated 03.02.1987 by nearly two and a half years, thereby satisfying the test of proximity.

Being a pre-notification transaction, Ex. A-4 reflects the prevailing market value prior to the initiation of acquisition proceedings and is not influenced by any speculative rise due to the proposed acquisition.
23. The evidence on record further establishes that the land covered under Ex. A-4 is situated abutting National Highway No.9 and in close vicinity to the RTC Bus Stand.
The acquired lands in Sy.Nos.787 and 789 are also located immediately adjacent to the RTC Bus Stand and abutting the same highway.
Thus, the locational advantage, access, and commercial potential of the land under Ex. A-4 are comparable to that of the acquired lands.
24. Moreover, Ex. A-4 is a registered document and its genuineness has not been seriously disputed.

There is no evidence to suggest that the transaction was either nominal or brought into existence A.P.S.R.T.C vs Tammara Ahalya on 5 March, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/65854664/
6 with an intention to inflate market value.
Though the extent covered is small, it is settled that small plot transactions can be taken as exemplars, subject to appropriate deductions towards development charges.
Hence, Ex. A-4 constitutes a relevant and reliable piece of evidence for assessing the market value of the acquired land as on the date of notification.

25. Insofar as the aspect of potentiality is concerned, reliance was placed by the learned counsel for the respondents on the judgment of the Honourable Supreme Court in Atma Singh (Dead) through LRs v. State of Haryana 6, which lays down that while determining market value, the Court must take into account not only the existing condition of the land but also its capacity for future development, having regard to its location, surroundings, and available amenities.

entities.text: Atma Singh (Dead) through LRs v. State of Haryana 6
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
The Relevant para is read as under:
"4. ...

The market value is the price that a willing purchaser would pay to a willing seller for the property having due regard to its existing condition with all its existing advantages and its potential possibilities when led out in most advantageous manner excluding any advantage due to carrying out of the scheme for which the property is compulsorily acquired.
In considering market value disinclination of the vendor to part with his land and the urgent necessity of the (2008) 2 SCC 568 purchaser to buy should be disregarded.

The guiding star would be the conduct of hypothetical willing vendor who would offer the land and a purchaser in normal human conduct would be willing to buy as a prudent man in normal market conditions but not an anxious dealing at arm's length nor facade of sale nor fictitious sale brought about in quick succession or otherwise to inflate the market value.
The determination of market value is the prediction of an economic event viz. a price outcome of hypothetical sale expressed in terms of probabilities.
5. For ascertaining the market value of the land, the potentiality of the acquired land should also be taken into consideration.
Potentiality means capacity or possibility for changing or developing into state of actuality.

It is well settled that market value of a property has to be determined having due regard to its existing condition with all its existing advantages and its potential possibility when led out in its most advantageous manner.

The question whether a land has potential value or not, is primarily one of fact depending upon its condition, situation, user to which it is put or is reasonably capable of being put and proximity to residential, commercial or industrial areas or institutions.

The existing amenities like water, electricity,
possibility of their further extension, whether near about town is developing or has prospect of development have to be taken into consideration..."
26.

It is well settled that while determining the market value of acquired land, the Court must take into consideration its existing geographical situation, present use, available advantages such as proximity to National or State Highways, developed areas, commercial centres, and the prevailing market value of lands situated in the same or adjacent locality, including the size of the land under acquisition.

The Honourable Supreme Court in Viluben Jhalejar Contractor v. State of Gujarat 7,
Executive Engineer, Karnataka Housing Board v. Land Acquisition Officer8, Bilkis v. State of A.P.S.R.T.C vs Tammara Ahalya on 5 March, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/65854664/
7 Maharashtra 9, and Sabhia Mohammed Yusuf Abdul Hamid Mulla v. Special Land Acquisition Officer 10, has consistently reiterated these guiding principles for determination of the market value of the lands acquired.

sentences.text: 27. Applying the above principle to the facts of the present case, this Court finds that the acquired lands, being situated abutting National Highway No.9 and immediately adjoining the existing RTC Bus Stand at Kodad, clearly possessed significant commercial and non-agricultural potential as on the date of the Section 4(1) notification.

Therefore, the Reference Court was justified in considering the advantageous location of the acquired lands abutting National Highway No.9 and situated within the developed limits of Kodad town, while determining the enhanced market value.

So far as the oral evidence is concerned, the depositions of PWs 1 to 6 not only establish the advantageous location of the acquired lands but also strongly support their commercial potential and the genuineness of Ex. A4. PW1, in his chief-examination, specifically deposed that the lands in Sy.Nos.787 and 789 are abutting National Highway No.9 and situated immediately adjacent to the existing RTC Bus Stand at Kodad, and that the surrounding area had already witnessed substantial development with educational institutions, shops, residential houses and government offices even prior to the Section 4(1) notification dated 03.02.1987.
This testimony clearly demonstrates that the lands possessed urban and commercial potential as on the relevant date.

29. Further, the evidence of PWs 2 to 6 corroborates the existence of developmental activities in the locality and affirms that the lands covered under Ex. A4 are situated in the same vicinity and share similar locational advantages.

The witnesses have spoken about the proximity of the exemplar land under Ex. A4 to the acquired land and its frontage on the Highway, thereby establishing comparability in terms of situation and potentiality.
Their depositions remained materially unshaken in cross-examination.
30. In contrast, the evidence adduced through RWs 1 and 2 does not effectively rebut the existence of development or the similarity between the acquired lands and the land covered under Ex. A4.

It is significant to note that RW2, during the course of cross-examination, categorically admitted that he had no personal knowledge with regard to the sale transactions covered under Exs.B2 to B5, which were produced on behalf of the appellant to rebut the version of the claimants that the acquired land is situated in a developed area.

Thus, the oral evidence of PWs 1 to 6 substantially supports to the conclusion that Ex. A4 is a genuine and comparable transaction and that the acquired lands possessed significant developmental and commercial potential as on the date of notification.

31. Insofar as the objection of the appellant that Ex. A4 relates to a smaller extent of land and therefore, cannot form the basis for determination of market value of a larger acquired extent, the said contention cannot be accepted in view of the settled legal position.

32. In Ravinder Kumar Goel v. State of Haryana and others 11, the Honourable Supreme Court had an occasion to consider whether 2023 SCC OnLine SC 147 transactions relating to smaller extents of land could be relied upon for determining the market value of large acquired tracts.

entities.text: Ravinder Kumar Goel v. State of Haryana and others
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
The Apex Court,
A.P.S.R.T.C vs Tammara Ahalya on 5 March, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/65854664/
8 while addressing this issue, observed as follows:
"13.

Therefore, since we have already indicated that the High Court was not justified in merely relying on the circular fixing the floor rates when other evidence was available on the record pursuant to the remand made, it is necessary for us to take note as to whether the Reference Court had committed an error in not relying on the sale exemplars produced by the respondents without analysing the comparability.

The position of law is well settled that when large extent of lands is acquired and if the sale exemplar, also for the large extentis available on record it would be safer to rely on the same if they are comparable transactions.
However, as already noted above, this Court in Atma Singh (supra) has also held that the sale instances of smaller extents cannot be ignored.
Further, this Court has reiterated in many cases that the sale exemplars for smaller extent can be relied upon subject to appropriate deduction being provided towards development charges."

33. Applying the above principle to the facts of the present case, Ex. A4, though relating to a smaller extent, pertains to land situated in the same locality, abutting National Highway No.9 and in close proximity to the acquired lands in Sy.Nos.787 and 789.

The Reference Court, while relying upon Ex.
A4, has already applied a deduction of 20% towards development charges.
Therefore, the reliance placed on Ex. A4 cannot be said to be improper or contrary to law.

34. On considering the question of deduction towards development charges, this Court finds that the Reference Court was justified in restricting the deduction to 20%, and the contention of the appellant seeking 40% deduction is untenable in the facts of the present case.
35. It is to be noted that the acquired lands are situated abutting National Highway No.9 and immediately adjacent to the existing RTC Bus Stand at Kodad.
The acquisition itself was for construction of an RTC Bus Depot and not for formation of a residential layout requiring extensive internal roads, drainage, parks, and other civic amenities.

When the land is already in a developed or semi-developed area with access to highway, electricity and surrounding infrastructure, a higher deduction rate of 40% which is applied to large tracts of undeveloped agricultural lands would not be appropriate.

36. In the present case, having regard to the existing development, locational advantages and the purpose of acquisition, the deduction of 20% towards developmental charges is reasonable and in consonance with settled principles.

Therefore, the plea of the appellant for application of 40%
deduction
is liable to be rejected.

IX. CONCLUSION:
37.

In light of the foregoing discussion, this Court is of the considered view that the Reference Court has acted on settled principles of law, appreciated the evidence correctly, and determined a fair market value of acquired lands at the rate of Rs. 141.12/- per sq. yard i.e., Rs. 5,57,568/- per acre.
The enhancement awarded by the learned Reference Court cannot be characterized either as excessive or arbitrary.

A.P.S.R.T.C vs Tammara Ahalya on 5 March, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/65854664/
9 38.

Therefore, for the reasons discussed hereinabove, in the absence of any material irregularity or perversity, this Court holds that the market value fixed by the Reference Court is just, fair and does not call for interference.
This Court further finds that the Reference Court has correctly appreciated the relevant factors while determining the market value as per the Act.

Further, the reliance placed on Ex. A4 as a comparable sale transaction is well-founded, particularly in light of the established proximity, similarity in location, and the proven commercial and developmental potential of the acquired lands in Sy.Nos.787 and 789 of Kodad.
The deduction of 20% towards development charges is reasonable and proportionate, having regard to the existing infrastructure and the purpose of acquisition.
The enhancement granted is neither excessive nor unsupported by the record.

Therefore, the impugned order of the Reference Court warrants no interference by this Court and the appellant failed to establish any of the grounds urged in the memorandum of appeal and thereby the appeal is devoid of merits and liable to be dismissed.

X. RESULT:
39.
In the light of the foregoing discussion, we find no merit in this appeal.
The judgment of the Reference Court does not call for interference.
The Claimants shall be entitled to all statutory benefits under the Act, including solatium, additional value and interest.
40. In result, the appeal stands dismissed.
In the circumstances, there shall be no order as to costs.
As a sequel, miscellaneous applications pending if any in this appeal, shall stand closed.

Applying the above principle to the facts of the present case, this Court finds that the acquired lands, being situated abutting National Highway No.9 and immediately adjoining the existing RTC Bus Stand at Kodad, clearly possessed significant commercial and non-agricultural potential as on the date of the Section 4(1) notification.
Therefore, the Reference Court was justified in considering the advantageous location of the acquired lands abutting National Highway No.9 and situated within the developed limits of Kodad town, while determining the enhanced market value.
31. Insofar as the objection of the appellant that Ex. A4 relates to a smaller extent of land and therefore, cannot form the basis for determination of market value of a larger acquired extent, the said contention cannot be accepted in view of the settled legal position.
The Reference Court, while relying upon Ex.
A4, has already applied a deduction of 20% towards development charges.
Therefore, the reliance placed on Ex. A4 cannot be said to be improper or contrary to law.
The acquisition itself was for construction of an RTC Bus Depot and not for formation of a residential layout requiring extensive internal roads, drainage, parks, and other civic amenities.
When the land is already in a developed or semi-developed area with access to highway, electricity and surrounding infrastructure, a higher deduction rate of 40% which is applied to large tracts of undeveloped agricultural lands would not be appropriate.
36. In the present case, having regard to the existing development, locational advantages and the purpose of acquisition, the deduction of 20% towards developmental charges is reasonable and in consonance with settled principles.
Therefore, the plea of the appellant for application of 40%
deduction
The enhancement awarded by the learned Reference Court cannot be characterized either as excessive or arbitrary.
The deduction of 20% towards development charges is reasonable and proportionate, having regard to the existing infrastructure and the purpose of acquisition.
The enhancement granted is neither excessive nor unsupported by the record.
Therefore, the impugned order of the Reference Court warrants no interference by this Court and the appellant failed to establish any of the grounds urged in the memorandum of appeal and thereby the appeal is devoid of merits and liable to be dismissed.
